stem: An ideal gas ($0.5$ mol), initially at $2$ bar pressure, is compressed at a constant temperature of $600$ K in two steps: first, against a constant external pressure of $P$ bar ($2 < P < 8$), and then against constant external pressure of $8$ bar. At each step, the compression is stopped only when the pressure of the gas becomes equal to the external pressure. The total work done on the gas in these steps is $W$. Considering all possible values of $P$ ($2 < P < 8$) and taking the gas constant as $R$ (in J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$), the minimum value of $|W|$ (in J) is

formulas: $W_{\mathrm{on}} = P_{\mathrm{ext}}(V_i - V_f)$ (work done ON the gas)
$V = nRT/P$ for ideal gas at constant $T$

steps.text: Work done ON the gas against constant external pressure: $W = P_{\mathrm{ext}}(V_i - V_f)$. Step 1: $P_{\mathrm{ext}} = P$, gas goes $2\ \mathrm{bar} \to P\ \mathrm{bar}$, so $W_1 = P\left(\frac{nRT}{2} - \frac{nRT}{P}\right) = nRT\left(\frac{P}{2} - 1\right)$.
Step 2: $P_{\mathrm{ext}} = 8$, gas goes $P \to 8$ bar, so $W_2 = 8\left(\frac{nRT}{P} - \frac{nRT}{8}\right) = nRT\left(\frac{8}{P} - 1\right)$.

Total $W = nRT\left(\frac{P}{2} + \frac{8}{P} - 2\right)$. Minimize $f(P) = \frac{P}{2} + \frac{8}{P} - 2$ on $(2, 8)$: $f'(P) = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{8}{P^2} = 0$ gives $P^2 = 16$, i.e. $P = 4$ (inside the interval); $f''(P) = 16/P^3 > 0$, so minimum. $f(4) = 2 + 2 - 2 = 2$.
$|W|_{\min} = 2nRT = 2(0.5)(R)(600) = 600R$ J. Matches option (B).

pitfalls: Using reversible work $nRT\ln(P_2/P_1)$ instead of irreversible $P_{\mathrm{ext}}\Delta V$
Sign errors: work done ON the gas is positive in compression
solution.final_check: Endpoints $P\to2$ and $P\to8$ both give $W = 900R > 600R$, confirming the interior minimum at $P=4$.

For a reversible reaction $\mathbf{R} ightleftharpoons \mathbf{P}$, at constant temperature, both the forward and the backward reactions are first order elementary reactions with rate constants $k_f$ and $k_b$, respectively. At time zero, the concentration of $\mathbf{R}$ is $[R]_0$ and the concentration of $\mathbf{P}$ is zero. At any given time, $[R]$ and $[P]$ are the concentrations of $\mathbf{R}$ and $\mathbf{P}$, respectively. If $k_b = 4k_f$, the correct graphical representation of the reaction is 
(A) $[R]/[R]_0$ (dashed) decays $1 	o 0.5$ and $[P]/[R]_0$ (solid) rises $0 	o 0.5$ 
(B) $[R]/[R]_0$ (dashed) decays $1 	o 0.2$ and $[P]/[R]_0$ (solid) rises $0 	o 0.8$ 
(C) $[R]/[R]_0$ (dashed) decays $1 	o 0.8$ and $[P]/[R]_0$ (solid) rises $0 	o 0.2$ 
(D) $[R]/[R]_0$ (dashed) decays toward $0$ and $[P]/[R]_0$ (solid) keeps rising past $1$ (no plateau)

steps.text: At equilibrium the forward and backward rates are equal: $k_f[R]_{eq} = k_b[P]_{eq}$. With $k_b = 4k_f$, $[R]_{eq} = 4[P]_{eq}$.

Both curves approach these plateaus monotonically (exponential approach, $[R]$ falling from $1$, $[P]$ rising from $0$). Only option (C) shows $[R]/[R]_0 \to 0.8$ and $[P]/[R]_0 \to 0.2$. (A) corresponds to $k_b = k_f$; (B) has the two swapped; (D) shows no equilibrium.

pitfalls: Swapping $[R]_{eq}$ and $[P]_{eq}$ (option B trap)
Forgetting mass balance
solution.final_check: Equilibrium constant $K = k_f/k_b = 1/4 = [P]_{eq}/[R]_{eq}$, so $[P]_{eq}:[R]_{eq} = 1:4$, i.e. 0.2 and 0.8 — option (C).

stem: The correct order of dipole moments for the given species is

steps.text: $\ce{BF3}$ is trigonal planar (symmetric) $\Rightarrow \mu = 0$. $\ce{NH4+}$ is tetrahedral (symmetric) $\Rightarrow \mu = 0$. So $\ce{BF3} = \ce{NH4+} = 0$.

In $\ce{NH3}$, the lone-pair dipole reinforces the N–H bond dipoles $\Rightarrow$ large $\mu$ ($\approx 1.47$ D). In $\ce{NF3}$, the lone-pair dipole opposes the N–F bond dipoles $\Rightarrow$ small net $\mu$ ($\approx 0.23$ D).
Hence $\ce{BF3} = \ce{NH4+} < \ce{NF3} < \ce{NH3}$, option (A).

pitfalls: Thinking $\ce{NF3} > \ce{NH3}$ because F is more electronegative (the lone pair direction reverses the net)
solution.final_check: $\mu(\ce{BF3})=\mu(\ce{NH4+})=0 < \mu(\ce{NF3})\approx0.23\ \mathrm{D} < \mu(\ce{NH3})\approx1.47\ \mathrm{D}$ — option (A).

stem: Considering $\ce{LiBH4}$ reduces an ester group to the corresponding alcohol and does not reduce a carboxylic acid group, the correct statement about the major products P, Q, R and S is \nSubstrate 1: cyclobutane with C1 bearing $\ce{EtO2C}$ (wedge) and $\ce{CO2H}$ (dash) on the same ring carbon, and $\ce{CH3}$ (wedge) on an adjacent ring carbon. P $\xleftarrow{1.\ \ce{LiBH4},\ 2.\ \ce{H+}}$ Substrate 1 $\xrightarrow{1.\ \ce{BH3},\ 2.\ \ce{H+}}$ Q. \nSubstrate 2: same constitution with $\ce{CH3}$ (wedge) on the ring carbon opposite the disubstituted carbon ($\ce{EtO2C}$ wedge, $\ce{CO2H}$ dash). R $\xleftarrow{1.\ \ce{LiBH4},\ 2.\ \ce{H+}}$ Substrate 2 $\xrightarrow{1.\ \ce{BH3},\ 2.\ \ce{H+}}$ S.

options.A: P & Q are identical, and R & S are diastereomers.
options.B: P & Q are diastereomers, and R & S are identical.
options.C: P & Q are diastereomers, and R & S are diastereomers.
options.D: P & Q are identical, and R & S are identical.

steps.text: $\ce{LiBH4}$ reduces only the ester: P = ring-C($\ce{CH2OH}$)( $\ce{CO2H}$), a hydroxy-ACID (formula $\ce{C7H12O3}$). $\ce{BH3}$ reduces only the acid: Q = ring-C($\ce{CO2Et}$)($\ce{CH2OH}$), a hydroxy-ESTER (formula $\ce{C9H16O3}$).

P and Q therefore have DIFFERENT constitutions (and different molecular formulas) — they are constitutional isomers, so strictly they can be neither 'identical' nor 'diastereomers' (diastereomers are stereoisomers, requiring identical connectivity). The same holds for R and S.

Hence none of (A)–(D) is strictly correct; the question is flawed as written. If the intended comparison ignored the $\ce{CO2H}$ vs $\ce{CO2Et}$ difference and only tracked the new $\ce{CH2OH}$ relative to $\ce{CH3}$ (cis in P, trans in Q), the intended answer would be (C).

pitfalls: Assuming P and Q have the same molecular formula without checking
solution.final_check: P ($\ce{C7H12O3}$, hydroxy-acid) vs Q ($\ce{C9H16O3}$, hydroxy-ester): different constitutions, so no option is strictly valid.

ambiguity: FLAWED QUESTION: P and Q (and R and S) are constitutional isomers (P is a hydroxy-acid, Q is a hydroxy-ester), not stereoisomers, so none of (A)-(D) is strictly correct. Recorded answer (C) is only the likely intended answer if the author overlooked the CO2H vs CO2Et constitution difference.

stem: The $2s$ and the $2p$ orbital energies of hydrogen atom are $E_{2s}(\mathrm{H})$ and $E_{2p}(\mathrm{H})$, respectively. The $2s$ and the $2p$ orbital energies of lithium atom are $E_{2s}(\mathrm{Li})$ and $E_{2p}(\mathrm{Li})$, respectively. The correct option(s) about the orbital energies is(are)

formulas: Multi-electron: $2s$ penetrates more than $2p$ $\Rightarrow E_{2s} < E_{2p}$

steps.text: (A) In Li (multi-electron), the $2s$ electron penetrates closer to the nucleus than $2p$, feels a larger $Z_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and lies lower: $E_{2s}(\mathrm{Li}) < E_{2p}(\mathrm{Li})$. TRUE.
(B) H has one electron; orbital energy depends only on $n$: $E_{2s}(\mathrm{H}) = E_{2p}(\mathrm{H}) = -13.6/4 = -3.4$ eV. TRUE.
(C) $E_{2p}(\mathrm{H}) = -3.4$ eV and $E_{2s}(\mathrm{Li}) \approx -5.39$ eV, so $E_{2p}(\mathrm{H}) > E_{2s}(\mathrm{Li})$. The stated $<$ is FALSE.
(D) $-3.4 > -5.39$, i.e. $E_{2s}(\mathrm{H}) > E_{2s}(\mathrm{Li})$. TRUE (Li's $2s$ is stabilized by $Z=3$).

pitfalls: Reversing inequality direction for negative energies
Forgetting penetration splits $2s/2p$ only in multi-electron atoms
solution.final_check: Numerically: $E_{2s}(H)=E_{2p}(H)=-3.4$ eV, $E_{2s}(Li)\approx-5.39$ eV $< E_{2p}(Li)$ — so A, B, D hold and C fails.

$\ce{NH3} + \mathbf{X}	ext{(excess)} \longrightarrow \mathbf{Y} + \ce{HCl}$

options.A: X is used for sterilizing drinking water.
options.C: Z is used in the enrichment of $^{235}$U.
options.D: Y is a stronger Lewis base than ammonia.

steps.text: X is the greenish-yellow gas from $\ce{MnO2}$/conc. HCl: $\ce{Cl2}$. (A) $\ce{Cl2}$ (chlorination) is used to sterilize drinking water. TRUE.

Since X ($\ce{Cl2}$) is in excess over $\ce{NH3}$: $\ce{NH3} + 3\ce{Cl2} \to \ce{NCl3} + \ce{3HCl}$, so Y = $\ce{NCl3}$ (nitrogen trichloride). (B) $\ce{NCl3}$ is trigonal pyramidal (like $\ce{NH3}$), not planar. FALSE.

Confusing ClF3 with UF6 for uranium enrichment

stem: Reaction of $\ce{PtF6}$ with oxygen ($\ce{O2}$) gas results in the formation of an ionic compound, $\mathbf{X^+Y^-}$. Correct statement(s) is(are)

options.B: Valence $d$-orbitals of the metal ion in $\mathbf{X^+Y^-}$ has $5$ electrons.
options.C: $\ce{PtF6}$ acts as an oxidant in this reaction.
options.D: $\ce{PtF6}$ acts as a fluorinating agent in this reaction.

steps.text: $\ce{PtF6}$ oxidizes $\ce{O2}$: $\ce{O2 + PtF6 -> [O2]+[PtF6]-}$ (Bartlett's discovery). So $\ce{X^+} = \ce{O2+}$ (dioxygenyl) and $\ce{Y^-} = \ce{PtF6-}$.
(A) $\ce{O2}$ has bond order $2$; removing one antibonding $\pi^*$ electron gives $\ce{O2+}$ with bond order $2.5$, not $1.5$. FALSE.
(B) In $\ce{PtF6-}$, Pt is in oxidation state $+5$ ($6 \times (-1) + x = -1$), i.e. $5d^5$. The valence $d$-orbitals hold $5$ electrons. TRUE.
(C) $\ce{PtF6}$ accepts an electron ($\ce{Pt(VI) -> Pt(V)}$) while oxidizing $\ce{O2}$; it acts as the oxidant. TRUE.
(D) No fluorine is transferred to oxygen; $\ce{PtF6}$ is not acting as a fluorinating agent here. FALSE.

pitfalls: Confusing O2+ (BO 2.5) with O2− (BO 1.5)
Miscounting Pt oxidation state in PtF6−
solution.final_check: $\ce{O2+}$: BO $= 2.5 \neq 1.5$; Pt(V) $= d^5$ ✓; $\ce{PtF6}$ is the oxidant ✓; no F-transfer ✗ — (B), (C).

options.A: S on warming with ammoniacal $\ce{AgNO3}$ results in the formation of silver mirror.
options.B: Q on treatment with $\ce{Cl2}$(excess)/UV gives gammaxane.
options.D: R on acid catalyzed intramolecular cyclization followed by treatment with Zn-Hg/HCl gives 9,10-dihydroxyanthracene.

steps.text: Kolbe's electrolysis of $\ce{CH3CH2CH2COO-}$ gives $n$-hexane, which under the stated $\ce{V2O5}$/500 °C conditions is converted to benzene: Q = benzene. (B) Benzene $+ \ce{Cl2}$(excess)/UV gives benzene hexachloride (gammaxane/BHC). TRUE — this also confirms Q is benzene.

Q (benzene) $+$ phthalic anhydride $\xrightarrow{\ce{AlCl3}}$ R = $o$-benzoylbenzoic acid (Friedel–Crafts acylation). R $\xrightarrow{\ce{PCl5}}$ acid chloride $\xrightarrow{\text{Rosenmund}}$ S = $o$-benzoylbenzaldehyde (2-benzoylbenzaldehyde).
(A) S contains an aldehyde ($\ce{-CHO}$), which reduces Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal $\ce{AgNO3}$) to a silver mirror on warming. TRUE.

(C) S $+ \ce{NH2NH2}$/heat: the aldehyde forms a hydrazone whose terminal $\ce{NH2}$ attacks the benzoyl ketone intramolecularly, closing a diazine ring — T = 1-phenylphthalazine, a heterocycle. TRUE.

(D) R ($o$-benzoylbenzoic acid) on intramolecular Friedel–Crafts cyclization gives anthraquinone (9,10-anthraquinone), and Clemmensen reduction (Zn-Hg/HCl) reduces $\ce{C=O \to CH2}$, giving anthracene — not 9,10-dihydroxyanthracene. FALSE.

pitfalls: Thinking Clemmensen gives an alcohol (it gives CH2)
Missing that gammaxane specifically identifies benzene
solution.final_check: Q=benzene→(B)✓; S=o-benzoylbenzaldehyde→Tollens ✓(A); T=1-phenylphthalazine, heterocyclic ✓(C); R→anthraquinone→anthracene, not a diol ✗(D).

stem: Two cylinders, both fitted with frictionless pistons, are filled with mixtures of He and Ar gases. In the first cylinder, the masses of He and Ar are $m_1$ and $m_2$, respectively. In the second cylinder, the masses of He and Ar are $m_2$ and $m_1$, respectively. The molar mass of Ar is $10$ times the molar mass of He. The external pressure applied by the piston on the first cylinder needs to be $5$ times that on the second cylinder so that the volume of the gas mixtures in both the cylinders are equal at the same temperature. Assuming He and Ar behave like ideal gases, the value of $(m_1/m_2)$ is ____.

steps.text: Let $M_{\ce{He}} = M$, so $M_{\ce{Ar}} = 10M$. Moles in cylinder 1: $n_1 = \frac{m_1}{M} + \frac{m_2}{10M} = \frac{10m_1 + m_2}{10M}$. Moles in cylinder 2: $n_2 = \frac{m_2}{M} + \frac{m_1}{10M} = \frac{10m_2 + m_1}{10M}$.
Same $V$ and $T$ with $P_1 = 5P_2$ gives $\frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{P_1}{P_2} = 5$, i.e. $\frac{10m_1 + m_2}{10m_2 + m_1} = 5$.

pitfalls: Using masses directly in place of moles
Swapping the two cylinders' compositions

stem: The total number of all possible isomers for the square planar complex with formula $\ce{K[M(NCS)(NO2)(gly)]}$ is ____. (M = metal ion and gly = $\ce{NH2CH2COO-}$)

formulas: Unsymmetrical bidentate $+$ 2 different monodentates in square planar: 2 geometrical isomers

steps.text: gly ($\ce{NH2CH2COO-}$) is an unsymmetrical bidentate (N and O donors) occupying two cis positions; $\ce{NCS-}$ and $\ce{NO2-}$ occupy the other two (mutually cis) positions.
Geometrical isomers: the gly N-atom can be trans to $\ce{NCS-}$ or trans to $\ce{NO2-}$ → 2 isomers.

Linkage isomers multiply independently: $\ce{NCS-}$ binds via N or S (2 ways); $\ce{NO2-}$ binds via N (nitro) or O (nitrito) (2 ways). Total $= 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$. (Square planar complexes are achiral, so no extra enantiomers.)

pitfalls: Forgetting linkage isomerism of NCS−/NO2−
Counting enantiomers for a planar complex
solution.final_check: 2 (geometric) × 2 (NCS linkage) × 2 (NO2 linkage) = 8 isomers.

stem: The sum of total number of carbonyl groups ($\ce{>C=O}$) present in the major products X and Y in the following reactions is ____. \n$\ce{HO2C-CH(CH3)-C(=O)-CH(CH3)-CO2H} \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} \mathbf{X}$ \ncis-3,4-dicarboxycyclopentanone $\xrightarrow{\text{heat}} \mathbf{Y}$

steps.text: X: $\ce{HOOC-CH(CH3)-CO-CH(CH3)-COOH}$ is a $\beta$-keto diacid (both $\ce{CO2H}$ beta to the ketone). On heating it undergoes double decarboxylation (cf. acetonedicarboxylic acid → acetone): X = $\ce{CH3CH2COCH2CH3}$ (pentan-3-one), which has 1 carbonyl group.

Y: the two $\ce{CO2H}$ groups are on adjacent ring carbons (cis) but gamma to the ring ketone, so no decarboxylation; instead the cis-1,2-diacid dehydrates on heating to the fused 5-membered cyclic anhydride. Carbonyls in Y: 1 (cyclopentanone) + 2 (anhydride) = 3. (Even unreacted, the count is 3.)

pitfalls: Counting only one decarboxylation for the diacid
Missing anhydride formation / miscounting C=O groups
solution.final_check: X = pentan-3-one (1 C=O); Y = cyclic anhydride (3 C=O); total = 4.

stem: Treatment of buta-1,3-diyne with $\ce{NaNH2}$ (2 equivalents), followed by reaction with excess of trans-$\ce{CH3-CH=CH-CH2-Br}$ gives X as the major product. The maximum number of carbon atoms that are collinear (in a straight line) in X is ____.

formulas: sp C: $180^\circ$; atoms bonded to sp C lie on the molecular axis

steps.text: 2 equiv $\ce{NaNH2}$ deprotonate both terminal alkynes: $\ce{^{-}C#C-C#C^{-}}$ (disodium salt). Excess trans-$\ce{CH3CH=CHCH2Br}$ alkylates both ends by SN2 at the $\ce{CH2Br}$ carbon: X = trans-$\ce{CH3CH=CH-CH2-C#C-C#C-CH2-CH=CH-CH3}$.

The four diyne carbons ($\ce{-C#C-C#C-}$) are sp and mutually collinear. Each terminal sp carbon is bonded to a $\ce{CH2}$ group along the same axis ($180^\circ$ at sp C), so both $\ce{CH2}$ carbons are also collinear: $4 + 2 = 6$ carbons.
The vinyl carbons branch off at tetrahedral ($\approx 109^\circ$) angles from the $\ce{CH2}$ groups and cannot be collinear with this axis. Maximum $= 6$.

pitfalls: Including the vinyl carbons (they bend away at the sp3 CH2)
Counting only the 4 diyne carbons
solution.final_check: Linear $\ce{CH2-C#C-C#C-CH2}$ unit = 6 collinear carbons; the alkenyl ends bend away — answer 6.

stem: List-I contains various physical/chemical processes, and List-II contains combinations of changes in enthalpy ($\Delta H$) and entropy ($\Delta S$). Match each entry in List-I to the appropriate entry in List-II, and choose the correct option. \nList-I: (P) Physisorption; (Q) Diamond $\longrightarrow$ Graphite; (R) Denaturation of protein; (S) Propene $\longrightarrow$ Cyclopropane \nList-II: (1) $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$; (2) $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$; (3) $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S = 0$; (4) $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$; (5) $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$

steps.text: (P) Physisorption: weak van der Waals binding is exothermic ($\Delta H < 0$); gas molecules lose translational freedom on the surface ($\Delta S < 0$) → (2).
(Q) Diamond → graphite: graphite is the stable allotrope ($\Delta H < 0$); the layered, softer graphite lattice has higher entropy than rigid diamond ($\Delta S > 0$) → (5).
(R) Denaturation (unfolding) breaks H-bonds/hydrophobic contacts ($\Delta H > 0$) and gives a disordered polypeptide ($\Delta S > 0$) → (1).
(S) Propene → cyclopropane (acyclic → strained ring): ring strain makes $\Delta H > 0$; cyclization reduces disorder ($\Delta S < 0$) → (4).
Combination P→2, Q→5, R→1, S→4 = option (C).

pitfalls: Assigning ΔS > 0 to adsorption
Getting the sign of ΔH for diamond→graphite wrong
solution.final_check: P→2, Q→5, R→1, S→4 matches only option (C).

Consider the following species: $\ce{SOCl2}$, $\ce{XeOF4}$, $\ce{ClF3}$, $\ce{ClF5}$, $\ce{XeF5+}$, $\ce{SO3^{2-}}$, $\ce{XeF3+}$, $\ce{SF4}$ 
List-I contains different molecular shapes and List-II contains total number of species with the same molecular shapes from the given species. Match each entry in List-I with the appropriate entry in List-II and choose the correct option. 
List-I: (P) See-saw; (Q) T-Shaped; (R) Trigonal Planar; (S) Square Pyramidal 
List-II: (1) one; (2) two; (3) three; (4) four; (5) zero

steps.text: Classify each (lone pairs on central atom): $\ce{SOCl2}$: 3 bonds + 1 lp → trigonal pyramidal; $\ce{XeOF4}$: 5 bonds + 1 lp → square pyramidal; $\ce{ClF3}$: 3 bonds + 2 lp → T-shaped; $\ce{ClF5}$: 5 bonds + 1 lp → square pyramidal; $\ce{XeF5+}$: 5 bonds + 1 lp → square pyramidal; $\ce{SO3^{2-}}$: 3 bonds + 1 lp → trigonal pyramidal; $\ce{XeF3+}$: 3 bonds + 2 lp → T-shaped; $\ce{SF4}$: 4 bonds + 1 lp → see-saw.

(P) See-saw: only $\ce{SF4}$ → (1) one. (Q) T-shaped: $\ce{ClF3}$, $\ce{XeF3+}$ → (2) two. (R) Trigonal planar: none ($\ce{SOCl2}$, $\ce{SO3^{2-}}$ are pyramidal) → (5) zero. (S) Square pyramidal: $\ce{XeOF4}$, $\ce{ClF5}$, $\ce{XeF5+}$ → (3) three.
P→1, Q→2, R→5, S→3 = option (A).

Calling SOCl2/SO3²⁻ trigonal planar

stem: The List-II contains products obtained from the reaction of compounds in List-I with $\ce{O3}$/Zn-$\ce{H2O}$ followed by cyclization (via more stable enolate) in the presence of aqueous $\ce{NaOH}$. Match each entry in List-I with appropriate entry in List-II and choose the correct option. \nList-I: (P) 6-6 fused alkene (double bond at fusion), $\ce{CH3}$ on each ring alpha to fusion; (Q) 7-5 fused alkene (double bond at fusion), $\ce{CH3}$ on 7-ring alpha to fusion-top and on 5-ring alpha to fusion-bottom; (R) 7-5 fused alkene (double bond at fusion), both $\ce{CH3}$ on the 7-ring alpha to the fusion atoms; (S) 6-6 fused alkene (double bond at fusion), both $\ce{CH3}$ on the same (left) ring alpha to the fusion atoms. \nList-II: (1)–(5) bicyclic hydroxy-ketones (aldol products); (1),(4),(5) are 6-6 fused, (2),(3) are 5-7 fused.

formulas: More substituted (methyl-bearing) $\alpha$-carbon gives the more stable enolate
Aldol: enolate C attacks the other C=O → new C–C bond; OH ends up on the attacked carbon

steps.text: Ozonolysis cleaves the fusion double bond: a 6-6 fused alkene gives a 10-membered 1,6-diketone; a 7-5 fused alkene gives a 10-membered 1,5-diketone. Intramolecular aldol via the more stable (methyl-bearing) enolate re-closes the ring: 6-6 substrates give 5-7 fused aldols, 7-5 substrates give 6-6 fused aldols (ring-size swap, 5/6-membered closure favored).

(P) 6-6 → 5-7 fused aldol; methyls end up one on the fusion carbon and one on the 7-ring alpha to the OH-bearing fusion carbon → (2). (S) 6-6 → 5-7 fused aldol; the second methyl is on the 5-ring alpha to the OH-bearing fusion carbon → (3).

(Q) 7-5 → 6-6 fused aldol via the C10 (methyl-bearing) enolate attacking C5: one 6-ring carries both the ketone (alpha to the $\ce{CH3}$-fusion) and the methyl (alpha to the OH-fusion); the other 6-ring is unsubstituted → (1). (R) 7-5 → 6-6 fused aldol: ketone alpha to the $\ce{CH3}$-fusion on one ring, methyl alpha to the OH-fusion on the other ring → (5).
P→2, Q→1, R→5, S→3 = option (C).

pitfalls: Forgetting the ring-size swap (6-6→5-7, 7-5→6-6)
Using the less stable (unsubstituted) enolate
solution.final_check: Ring-size swap plus methyl tracking gives P→2, Q→1, R→5, S→3 — option (C), the only option with P→2 and S→3.

stem: Consider the function $f:(0, \infty) \to (-\infty, \infty)$ given by $f(x) = \sqrt{x}\,\log_e(x) - x + 1$. Then which one of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: The derivative of the function $f$ is decreasing in the interval $(0, 1)$
options.B: The function $f$ has a local maximum at some point $M \in (0, \infty)$
options.C: The function $f$ has a local minimum at some point $m \in (0, \infty)$
options.D: The function $f$ has NEITHER a point of local maximum NOR a point of local minimum in the interval $(0, \infty)$

steps.text: Differentiate: $f'(x) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\ln x + \sqrt{x}\cdot\frac{1}{x} - 1 = \frac{\ln x}{2\sqrt{x}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} - 1$. Differentiating again, $f''(x) = -\frac{\ln x}{4x^{3/2}}$.
On $(0,1)$, $\ln x < 0$, so $f''(x) > 0$; hence $f'$ is INCREASING on $(0,1)$. Option (A) is FALSE.

$f'(x) = 0 \iff \frac{\ln x}{2} + 1 = \sqrt{x}$. Put $g(x) = \frac{\ln x}{2} + 1 - \sqrt{x}$; then $g'(x) = \frac{1-\sqrt{x}}{2x}$, so $g$ increases on $(0,1)$, decreases on $(1,\infty)$, with maximum $g(1) = 0$. Thus $g(x) < 0$ for all $x \ne 1$, i.e. $f'(x) < 0$ for every $x \ne 1$ (and $f'(1) = 0$).

Since $f'$ is negative on both sides of the lone critical point $x = 1$, $f$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$ and has no local maximum or minimum. Options (B) and (C) are FALSE; option (D) is TRUE.

pitfalls: Do not conclude an extremum from $f'(1) = 0$ alone: the sign of $f'$ does not change at $x = 1$.
solution.final_check: $f'(x) < 0$ for all $x \ne 1$, so $f$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$: only (D) can hold.

With $\theta = \tan^{-1} 2$: $\sin 2\theta = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1 + \tan^2\theta} = \frac{4}{5}$, so $10\sin(2\tan^{-1}2) = 8$.
Total: $(4\pi - 11) + 10 + 8 = 4\pi + 7$. Option (C).

stem: Suppose that Box I contains $6$ red balls and $9$ green balls, and Box II contains $8$ red balls and $12$ green balls. All the balls of Box I and Box II are mixed together and a ball is chosen at random from them. Let $B_1$ be the event that the ball chosen belonged to Box I and let $B_2$ be the event that the ball chosen belonged to Box II. Let $R_1$ be the event that the ball chosen is red and let $R_2$ be the event that the ball chosen is green. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?

options.C: The conditional probability $P(R_1 \mid B_1)$ is equal to the conditional probability $P(R_1 \mid B_2)$
options.D: The conditional probability $P(R_1 \mid B_1)$ is greater than the conditional probability $P(R_2 \mid B_2)$

formulas: Events $E, F$ independent $\iff P(E \cap F) = P(E)P(F)$

steps.text: Totals: Box I has $15$ balls, Box II has $20$ balls; mixed pool has $14$ red and $21$ green ($35$ total).
(A): $P(B_1 \cap R_1) = \frac{6}{35}$ and $P(B_1)P(R_1) = \frac{3}{7}\cdot\frac{2}{5} = \frac{6}{35}$. Equal, so $B_1$ and $R_1$ are INDEPENDENT. (A) is TRUE.
(B): $P(B_2 \cap R_2) = \frac{12}{35}$ and $P(B_2)P(R_2) = \frac{4}{7}\cdot\frac{3}{5} = \frac{12}{35}$. Equal, so $B_2$ and $R_2$ are independent, NOT dependent. (B) is FALSE.
(C): $P(R_1 \mid B_1) = \frac{6}{15} = \frac{2}{5}$ and $P(R_1 \mid B_2) = \frac{8}{20} = \frac{2}{5}$. Equal (both boxes have the same red fraction). (C) is TRUE.
(D): $P(R_1 \mid B_1) = \frac{2}{5}$ versus $P(R_2 \mid B_2) = \frac{12}{20} = \frac{3}{5}$; $\frac{2}{5} > \frac{3}{5}$ is false. (D) is FALSE.

pitfalls: The equal red fractions ($6/15 = 8/20$) make box-origin independent of colour; verify each option numerically rather than by intuition.

stem: Let $\Pi$ be the plane such that it contains the straight line $\frac{x-1}{2} = \frac{y-3}{3} = \frac{z+2}{1}$ and is perpendicular to the plane $x + 2y + 3z = 4$. Let $\Pi_1$ be the plane which passes through the point $(4, 2, 2)$ and is parallel to $\Pi$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?

options.A: The equation of the plane $\Pi$ is $7x - 5y + z = -10$
options.B: The distance between the planes $\Pi$ and $\Pi_1$ is $30$
options.C: The distance of the plane $\Pi$ from the origin is $2\sqrt{3}$
options.D: The acute angle between the plane $\Pi$ and the plane $2x + 2y + z = 3$ is $\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\right)$

steps.text: Direction of the line $\vec{d} = (2, 3, 1)$; normal of $x + 2y + 3z = 4$ is $\vec{n_1} = (1, 2, 3)$. Normal of $\Pi$: $\vec{n} = \vec{d} \times \vec{n_1} = (3\cdot3 - 1\cdot2,\ 1\cdot1 - 2\cdot3,\ 2\cdot2 - 3\cdot1) = (7, -5, 1)$.
$\Pi$ passes through $(1, 3, -2)$ (point on the line): $7(x-1) - 5(y-3) + (z+2) = 0$, i.e. $7x - 5y + z = -10$. (A) is TRUE.
$\Pi_1 \parallel \Pi$ through $(4,2,2)$: $7x - 5y + z = 28 - 10 + 2 = 20$. Distance $= \frac{|20 - (-10)|}{\sqrt{49 + 25 + 1}} = \frac{30}{5\sqrt{3}} = 2\sqrt{3} \ne 30$. (B) is FALSE.
Distance of $\Pi$ from origin $= \frac{|-10|}{\sqrt{75}} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \ne 2\sqrt{3}$. (C) is FALSE.
Acute angle between $\Pi$ and $2x + 2y + z = 3$: $\cos\theta = \frac{|(7,-5,1)\cdot(2,2,1)|}{\sqrt{75}\cdot 3} = \frac{|14 - 10 + 1|}{15\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}$. (D) is TRUE.

pitfalls: For (B): $30$ is the numerator before dividing by $\sqrt{75} = 5\sqrt{3}$; do not forget the normalisation.
solution.final_check: $\Pi: 7x-5y+z=-10$ verified through $(1,3,-2)$; distances $2\sqrt3$, $2/\sqrt3$; $\cos\theta = 1/(3\sqrt3)$.

stem: Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the set of all real numbers. Let $f:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be an arbitrary function and let $g:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the function defined by $g(x) = xf(x)$, for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?

options.A: The function $g$ is always continuous at $x = 0$
options.B: If $f$ is continuous at $x = 0$, then $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$
options.C: If $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$, then $f$ is continuous at $x = 0$
options.D: If $g$ is differentiable at $x = 0$, then $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)$ exists

steps.text: (A) is FALSE. Counterexample: $f(x) = 1/x$ for $x \ne 0$, $f(0) = 0$. Then $g(x) = 1$ for $x \ne 0$ but $g(0) = 0$; $g$ is discontinuous at $0$. (The factor $x$ need not tame an arbitrary $f$.)
(B) is TRUE. $g(0) = 0$, and $\frac{g(h) - g(0)}{h} = f(h)$ for $h \ne 0$; if $f$ is continuous at $0$, this tends to $f(0)$, so $g'(0) = f(0)$ exists.

(C) is FALSE. Counterexample: $f(x) = 1$ for $x \ne 0$, $f(0) = 0$. Then $g(x) = x$ everywhere, differentiable at $0$, but $f$ is discontinuous at $0$ (limit $1 \ne f(0) = 0$). Differentiability of $g$ at $0$ says nothing about the value $f(0)$.
(D) is TRUE. Differentiability of $g$ at $0$ means $\lim_{h \to 0}\frac{g(h)-g(0)}{h}$ exists; for $h \ne 0$ this quotient equals $f(h)$, so $\lim_{x \to 0} f(x)$ exists (and equals $g'(0)$).

pitfalls: Distinguish (C) from (D): differentiability of $g$ at $0$ forces the LIMIT of $f$ to exist, but $f(0)$ itself is unconstrained, so continuity of $f$ need not follow.
solution.final_check: Counterexamples kill (A) and (C); the difference quotient $\frac{g(h)}{h} = f(h)$ ($h\ne0$) proves (B) and (D).

stem: Consider the matrix $M = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$. Let $a, b, c, d, m, n, p$ and $q$ be integers such that $M^{26} = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{26} M^k = \begin{pmatrix} m & n \\ p & q \end{pmatrix}$. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?

options.A: There exists a $2 \times 2$ invertible matrix $P$ with real entries such that $MP = P\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$
options.C: For any two given integers $r$ and $s$, there exist unique integers $x$ and $y$ such that $ax + by = r$ and $cx + dy = s$
options.D: For each positive real number $t$, the system of linear equations $(m+t)x + ny = 1$, $px + (q+t)y = -1$ has a unique solution

steps.text: $M - I = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix} = N$ with $N^2 = 0$. Hence $M^k = (I+N)^k = I + kN = \begin{pmatrix} 1+k & -k \\ k & 1-k \end{pmatrix}$. So $M^{26} = \begin{pmatrix} 27 & -26 \\ 26 & -25 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{26} M^k = 26I + \left(\sum_{k=1}^{26}k\right)N = 26I + 351N = \begin{pmatrix} 377 & -351 \\ 351 & -325 \end{pmatrix}$. Thus $m = 377 \ne 378$: (B) is FALSE.

(A): $M = I + N$ with $N \ne 0$, $N^2 = 0$ (rank-$1$ nilpotent). Every nonzero $2\times2$ nilpotent is similar over $\mathbb{R}$ to $\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$; e.g. with $P = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ ($\det P = -1$), $NP = P\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, so $MP = P\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. (A) is TRUE.

(C): $\det M^{26} = (\det M)^{26} = 1^{26} = 1$. An integer matrix with determinant $\pm 1$ is invertible over $\mathbb{Z}$, so $M^{26} : \mathbb{Z}^2 \to \mathbb{Z}^2$ is bijective: unique integer $(x, y)$ for every integer $(r, s)$. (C) is TRUE.

(D): The system matrix is $S + tI$ with $S = \begin{pmatrix} 377 & -351 \\ 351 & -325 \end{pmatrix}$. $\det(S + tI) = (377+t)(-325+t) + 351^2 = t^2 + 52t + 676 = (t+26)^2 > 0$ for all $t > 0$. Nonzero determinant $\Rightarrow$ unique solution. (D) is TRUE.

pitfalls: For (B), compute $m$ from the sum formula rather than guessing: $m = 26 + 351 = 377$. For (D), note $(t+26)^2 = 0$ only at $t = -26$, never for $t > 0$.
solution.final_check: $M^{26} = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}27&-26\\26&-25\end{smallmatrix}\right]$, $\sum M^k = \left[\begin{smallmatrix}377&-351\\351&-325\end{smallmatrix}\right]$; (B) fails on $377 \ne 378$; (A),(C),(D) verified.

stem: Let $S = \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 10\}$. Consider the set $B = \{R : R \text{ is an equivalence relation on the set } S \text{ such that } R \text{ has exactly } 42 \text{ elements}\}$. Then the number of elements in $B$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

formulas: If blocks have sizes $n_1, \ldots, n_k$: $|R| = \sum n_i^2$, $\sum n_i = 10$
Number of partitions with given block sizes: $\frac{10!}{n_1!\cdots n_k! \cdot (\text{multiplicities})!}$

steps.text: An equivalence relation with block sizes $n_1, \ldots, n_k$ ($\sum n_i = 10$) has $|R| = \sum n_i^2$ ordered pairs. Need $\sum n_i^2 = 42$ with $\sum n_i = 10$.
Block sizes $\{6,2,1,1\}$: $\frac{10!}{6!\,2!\,1!\,1!\,2!} = \frac{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7}{4} = 1260$ (dividing by $2!$ for the two singleton blocks).

pitfalls: Remember $R$ counts ORDERED pairs ($n_i^2$ per block, not $\binom{n_i}{2}$); and divide by factorials of repeated block sizes.
solution.final_check: Two valid block-size types, $1260$ partitions each: $2520$ equivalence relations.

stem: Consider the function $f:\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \to (-\infty, \infty)$ defined by $f(x) = (|x| + |x - 1|)\sin x + [x\sin x]$, where $[x\sin x]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x\sin x$. Let $\alpha$ be the total number of points in the interval $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ at which $f$ is NOT continuous, and let $\beta$ be the total number of points in the interval $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$ at which $f$ is NOT differentiable. Then the value of $\alpha + \beta$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

formulas: $[t]$ jumps exactly where $t$ crosses an integer
$x\sin x$ is even, $0 \le x\sin x < \frac{\pi}{2}$ on $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$

steps.text: Split $f = g + h$ with $g(x) = (|x| + |x-1|)\sin x$ (continuous everywhere) and $h(x) = [x\sin x]$. On $\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)$, $x\sin x \ge 0$ is even, strictly decreasing on $(-\pi/2, 0)$ from $\pi/2$ to $0$ and strictly increasing on $(0, \pi/2)$ from $0$ to $\pi/2$. Since $\pi/2 \approx 1.57$, $x\sin x$ crosses the integer $1$ exactly once on each side: two jump points $\pm a$ ($a\sin a = 1$). Hence $f$ is discontinuous at exactly $2$ points: $\alpha = 2$.
Non-differentiability: the points $\pm a$ are already non-differentiable (discontinuous). Elsewhere $h$ is locally constant, so check kinks of $g$ at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$.

At $x = 0$: for $x < 0$ small, $g(x) = (1-2x)\sin x$ with derivative $-2\sin x + (1-2x)\cos x \to 1$; for $x > 0$ small, $g(x) = \sin x$ with derivative $\cos x \to 1$. Equal, so $g$ (hence $f$) IS differentiable at $0$.

At $x = 1$: left derivative $= \cos 1$ (since $g = \sin x$ on $(0,1)$); right derivative $= 2\sin 1 + \cos 1 \ne \cos 1$ (since $g = (2x-1)\sin x$ on $(1, \pi/2)$). So $f$ is not differentiable at $x = 1$. Thus $\beta = 2 + 1 = 3$, and $\alpha + \beta = 5$.

pitfalls: The subtle point: the kink of $|x|$ at $0$ does NOT break differentiability here (left and right derivatives coincide); only $|x-1|$ at $x=1$ does.
solution.final_check: $\alpha = 2$ (floor jumps), $\beta = 3$ ($\pm a$ plus $x=1$): $\alpha + \beta = 5$.

ambiguity: Source extraction contained stray '2 2' fragments near the function definition (possibly a misplaced sin(2x/pi) or exponents). Solved under the clean reading f(x) = (|x|+|x-1|) sin x + [x sin x] on (-pi/2, pi/2); the alternative reading with sin(2x/pi) yields the same alpha+beta = 5.

stem: The number of ways to distribute $10$ identical red pens and $14$ identical blue pens among four persons such that each person gets $6$ pens, is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

formulas: Nonnegative solutions of $r_1 + r_2 + r_3 + r_4 = 10$: $\binom{13}{3}$

steps.text: Let $r_i$ = red pens for person $i$. Since each person gets $6$ pens total and there are $10 + 14 = 24 = 4 \times 6$ pens, it suffices to count $r_1 + r_2 + r_3 + r_4 = 10$ with $0 \le r_i \le 6$ (blue counts are then forced: $b_i = 6 - r_i$, and $\sum b_i = 14$ automatically).
Unconstrained nonnegative solutions: $\binom{10+4-1}{4-1} = \binom{13}{3} = 286$.

Subtract solutions with some $r_i \ge 7$: put $r_i' = r_i - 7 \ge 0$, then $r_i' + (\text{other three}) = 3$, giving $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ per choice of $i$, i.e. $4 \times 20 = 80$. Two variables cannot both be $\ge 7$ (sum would exceed $10$).
Valid distributions: $286 - 80 = 206$.

pitfalls: The upper bound $r_i \le 6$ is essential: forgetting it gives $286$, a classic trap.

stem: Let $\alpha = \left(1 - 2\cos\frac{\pi}{11}\right)\left(1 - 2\cos\frac{3\pi}{11}\right)\left(1 - 2\cos\frac{9\pi}{11}\right)\left(1 - 2\cos\frac{27\pi}{11}\right)\left(1 - 2\cos\frac{81\pi}{11}\right)$. Then the value of $\frac{5 - \alpha}{2}$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_.

steps.text: Reduce the angles: $\frac{27\pi}{11} = 2\pi + \frac{5\pi}{11}$ and $\frac{81\pi}{11} = 8\pi - \frac{7\pi}{11}$, so the five factors use $\theta_j = \frac{(2j+1)\pi}{11}$ for $j = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ (i.e. $\pi/11, 3\pi/11, 5\pi/11, 7\pi/11, 9\pi/11$).

Identity: $\sin\frac{3\theta}{2} = \sin\frac{\theta}{2}(1 + 2\cos\theta)$, so $1 + 2\cos\theta = \frac{\sin(3\theta/2)}{\sin(\theta/2)}$; replacing $\theta \to \theta + \pi$ gives $1 - 2\cos\theta = -\frac{\cos(3\theta/2)}{\cos(\theta/2)}$ (check: $\theta = 0$ gives $-1 = -1$).

Hence $\alpha = (-1)^5 \prod_{j=0}^{4}\frac{\cos(3(2j+1)\pi/22)}{\cos((2j+1)\pi/22)}$. The numerator angles are $\frac{3\pi}{22}, \frac{9\pi}{22}, \frac{15\pi}{22}, \frac{21\pi}{22}, \frac{27\pi}{22}$, and $\cos\frac{15\pi}{22} = -\cos\frac{7\pi}{22}$, $\cos\frac{21\pi}{22} = -\cos\frac{\pi}{22}$, $\cos\frac{27\pi}{22} = -\cos\frac{5\pi}{22}$. So the numerator product $= -\prod_{j=0}^{4}\cos\frac{(2j+1)\pi}{22}$, exactly $-1$ times the denominator.
Therefore $\alpha = (-1)\cdot(-1) = 1$, and $\frac{5 - \alpha}{2} = \frac{4}{2} = 2$.

pitfalls: Reduce $27\pi/11$ and $81\pi/11$ modulo $2\pi$ first; the five angles are then the odd multiples of $\pi/11$ below $\pi$.

stem: Consider a large disk of radius $R$ and two smaller disks, each of radius $r = R/50$, lying on its circumference, as shown in the figure. The smaller disks are initially in contact with each other, with an angular separation $\Delta\phi$ between their centres. They are made to roll without slipping in opposite directions, with constant angular velocities $\omega$ and $2\omega$ while the large disk is held stationary. The time $t$ at which the smaller disks are again in contact is: [Use $\sin(\Delta\phi) = \Delta\phi$ and ignore gravity.]

steps.text: Each small-disk centre moves on a circle of radius $R + r = 51r$ about the large-disk centre. Rolling without slipping on the stationary large disk means the contact point is instantaneously at rest, so each centre has tangential speed $v = \omega_{spin}\,r$.

Hence the orbital angular speeds about the large-disk centre are $\Omega_1 = \omega r/(R+r) = \omega/51$ and $\Omega_2 = 2\omega r/(R+r) = 2\omega/51$, in opposite senses. The spin $\omega$ is reduced by the factor $r/(R+r) = 1/51$.

Initial contact: the centres are a chord $2r$ apart on the circle of radius $R+r$, so $2(R+r)\sin(\Delta\phi/2) = 2r$, i.e. $\sin(\Delta\phi/2) = 1/51$. With $\sin x \simeq x$, $\Delta\phi \simeq 2/51$.

The disks roll apart from each other and touch again once their relative angular separation has grown through $2\pi - \Delta\phi$. Relative rate $= \Omega_1 + \Omega_2 = 3\omega/51$, so $t = (2\pi - \Delta\phi)/(3\omega/51) = 51(2\pi - \Delta\phi)/(3\omega)$, with $\Delta\phi = 2/51$.

pitfalls: Using the spin $\omega$ directly as the orbital rate (missing the $1/51$ reduction from rolling on the large circle).
Using $\Delta\phi$ instead of $2\pi - \Delta\phi$: the disks separate first and meet again after nearly a full turn.
solution.final_check: Relative rate $3\omega/51$ over $\approx 2\pi$ gives $t \approx 34\pi/\omega$; only the $/3\omega$, $(2\pi-\Delta\phi)$ option matches. NOTE: option letters reconstructed from garbled OCR; the verified formula is $t = 51(2\pi-\Delta\phi)/(3\omega)$.

stem: Consider a circuit consisting of a capacitor of capacitance $C$ and a coil with $n$ turns per unit length, cross sectional area $A$ and length $l$, where $l^2 \gg A$. There is another coil of length $l/2$, cross sectional area $A/2$ and $2n$ turns per unit length completely inside the larger coil, as shown in the figure. The ends of this smaller coil are connected with each other by an insulated conducting wire. The self-inductance of the larger coil is $L$. Neglecting edge effects and all the Ohmic resistances, the resonant frequency of the circuit is:

concepts: Self and mutual inductance of solenoids

steps.text: Large coil: $L_1 = \mu_0 n^2 A l = L$ (given). Small coil: turns/length $2n$, area $A/2$, length $l/2$, so $L_2 = \mu_0(2n)^2(A/2)(l/2) = \mu_0 n^2 A l = L$.
Mutual inductance (small coil fully inside, flux linkage over its whole length): $M = \mu_0\,n\,(2n)\,(A/2)\,(l/2) = \mu_0 n^2 A l/2 = L/2$.

The small coil is shorted with zero resistance: $i\omega L_2 I_2 + i\omega M I_1 = 0$, so $I_2 = -(M/L_2)I_1$. Voltage at the large-coil terminals: $V = i\omega L_1 I_1 + i\omega M I_2 = i\omega\,(L_1 - M^2/L_2)\,I_1$. Effective inductance $L_{eff} = L - (L/2)^2/L = 3L/4$.
Resonance of the capacitor with this effective inductance: $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{L_{eff} C} = 1/\sqrt{3LC/4} = 2/\sqrt{3LC}$.

pitfalls: Using $L$ instead of the reduced $L_{eff}$: the shorted inner coil opposes flux and lowers the inductance.
Sign error in the reflected term: it is $-M^2/L_2$ (Lenz's law), not $+$.
solution.final_check: $L_2 = L$, $M = L/2$ give $L_{eff} = 3L/4$ and $\omega_0 = 2/\sqrt{3LC}$. NOTE: option letters reconstructed from merged OCR; the verified value is $2/\sqrt{3LC}$.

stem: A solid cylinder of radius $R$ rolls without slipping with a centre-of-mass speed $v_0 = \sqrt{gR/3}$ on a horizontal surface with a vertical edge, as shown in the figure. Here, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. At the moment when the cylinder loses contact with the surface due to rotation around the corner, the speed of its centre of mass is:

concepts: Conservation of angular momentum about the corner (impulsive pivot)
Loss of contact: normal reaction vanishes
formulas: $L_{corner}$ conserved at the pivot: $\frac32 m v_0 R = \frac32 m R^2\omega'$

steps.text: Just before the edge the cylinder rolls without slipping: $\omega_0 = v_0/R$. At the instant it starts pivoting about the corner, the only impulsive force acts at the corner, so angular momentum about the corner is conserved: $m v_0 R + I_{cm}\omega_0 = I_{corner}\,\omega'$, i.e. $\frac32 m v_0 R = \frac32 mR^2\omega'$, giving $\omega' = v_0/R$.
Rotating about the fixed corner through angle $\theta$ from the vertical, energy conservation gives $\frac12(\frac32 mR^2)(\omega^2 - \omega'^2) = mgR(1 - \cos\theta)$.
Contact with the corner is lost when its normal reaction vanishes: radially $mg\cos\theta - N = m\omega^2 R$, so $\omega^2 R = g\cos\theta$ at loss of contact.

Eliminating $\omega$: $\frac34(g\cos\theta - v_0^2/R) = g(1-\cos\theta)$, so $\cos\theta = \frac47 + \frac{3v_0^2}{7gR}$. With $v_0^2 = gR/3$: $\cos\theta = \frac47 + \frac17 = \frac57$. Centre-of-mass speed $v = \omega R = \sqrt{gR\cos\theta} = \sqrt{5gR/7}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the spin contribution $I_{cm}\omega_0$ in the angular momentum about the corner just before pivoting.
Using energy about the centre of mass instead of about the fixed corner during the tipping phase.
solution.final_check: $\cos\theta = 5/7 < 1$ is physical, and $v = \sqrt{5gR/7}$. NOTE: the stem's $v_0$ was OCR-garbled; $v_0 = \sqrt{gR/3}$ is the reading consistent with a physical ($\cos\theta\le 1$) answer and the option fragment $\sqrt{5gR/7}$; option letters reconstructed best-effort.

stem: Consider a hydrogen atom with $v_n$, $r_n$, and $K_n$ denoting the velocity, orbital radius and kinetic energy of the electron in the $n$th orbit, respectively. The electron undergoes a transition from the $n$th orbit, emitting radiation corresponding to the Lyman series. Considering $h$ to be the Planck's constant and $\varepsilon_0$ the permittivity of the free space, the correct statement(s) is/are:

options.A: Magnitude of change in kinetic energy of electron can be expressed as $\left|\dfrac{h}{4\pi}\left(\dfrac{nv_n}{r_n} - \dfrac{v_1}{r_1}\right)\right|$.
options.B: Magnitude of change in de Broglie wavelength of the electron can be expressed as $\dfrac{h^2}{4\varepsilon_0}\left|\dfrac{1}{K_n} - \dfrac{1}{K_1}\right|$.
options.C: Frequency of the radiation emitted can be expressed as $\dfrac{h^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 h}\left(\dfrac{1}{r_1} - \dfrac{1}{r_n}\right)$.
options.D: Magnitude of change in total energy of the electron can be expressed as $\left|\dfrac{h}{2\pi}\left(\dfrac{v_1}{r_1} - \dfrac{nv_n}{r_n}\right)\right|$.

steps.text: (A) From $m v_n r_n = nh/2\pi$: $\frac{h}{4\pi}\frac{nv_n}{r_n} = \frac{m v_n r_n}{2n}\frac{nv_n}{r_n} = \frac12 m v_n^2 = K_n$. So the expression equals $|K_n - K_1|$, exactly the magnitude of KE change. TRUE.

(B) $\lambda_n = h/p_n = h/\sqrt{2mK_n}$, so $|\Delta\lambda| = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m}}|1/\sqrt{K_n} - 1/\sqrt{K_1}|$. The given $\frac{h^2}{4\varepsilon_0}|1/K_n - 1/K_1|$ is dimensionally wrong (not a length) and functionally wrong. FALSE.

(C) As transcribed, the prefactor is $h^2/(8\pi\varepsilon_0 h) = h/(8\pi\varepsilon_0)$, which is dimensionally not a frequency per unit $1/r$; the correct formula has $e^2$ (elementary charge squared) in place of $h^2$: $\nu = \frac{e^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0 h}(1/r_1 - 1/r_n)$. As written: FALSE. (If the numerator is actually $e^2$ mis-OCRed, it is TRUE.)

(D) $\frac{h}{2\pi}(v_1/r_1) = 2K_1$ and $\frac{h}{2\pi}(nv_n/r_n) = 2K_n$ (twice the result in step 1), so the expression equals $2|K_1 - K_n|$. But $|\Delta E_{total}| = |(-K_1) - (-K_n)| = |K_1 - K_n|$ — off by a factor of 2. FALSE.

pitfalls: Confusing total energy with kinetic energy: $E_n = -K_n$, so $|\Delta E| = |\Delta K|$ but the prefactors must still match.
In (C), not checking dimensions: $h^2/(\varepsilon_0 h r)$ is not a frequency.
solution.final_check: Only (A) is an exact identity. Answer [A]. AMBIGUITY: if option (C)'s numerator is $e^2$ (OCR confusion), (C) is also correct and the answer would be [A, C].

stem: A particle is thrown with a speed $v$ from a point $P$ at an angle $\theta$ with the horizontal plane such that it passes through the point $Q$ at a height of $1\ \mathrm{m}$ and horizontal distance of $5\ \mathrm{m}$ from $P$, as shown in the figure. If acceleration due to gravity is $g\ \mathrm{ms^{-2}}$, then the correct statement(s) is/are:

options.B: If $\theta = 45^\circ$, the particle reaches its maximum height before it reaches $Q$.
options.C: If $\theta = 30^\circ$, the particle reaches its maximum height after reaching $Q$.

steps.text: (A) Put $(x, y) = (5, 1)$, $\theta = 45^\circ$ in the trajectory: $1 = 5(1) - \frac{g\cdot 25}{2v^2(1/2)} = 5 - \frac{25g}{v^2}$. Hence $25g/v^2 = 4$, $v^2 = 25g/4$, $v = 5\sqrt{g}/2\ \mathrm{m/s}$. TRUE.
(B) With this $v$: $x_{max} = v^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g = (25g/4)(1/2)/g = 25/8 = 3.125\ \mathrm{m} < 5\ \mathrm{m}$. Maximum height is attained before $x = 5$ m, i.e. before $Q$. TRUE.

(C) For $\theta = 30^\circ$ through $Q$: $1 = 5\tan30^\circ - \frac{25g}{2v^2\cos^2 30^\circ} = 5/\sqrt{3} - \frac{50g}{3v^2}$, giving $v^2 = \frac{50g}{3(5/\sqrt{3}-1)} \approx 8.83g$. Then $x_{max} = v^2\sin30^\circ\cos30^\circ/g \approx 8.83(0.433) \approx 3.83\ \mathrm{m} < 5\ \mathrm{m}$: maximum height is reached BEFORE $Q$, so 'after reaching Q' is FALSE.

(D) With $\tan\theta = 1/5$, the line of projection from $P$ passes exactly through $Q$ ($y = x/5$ gives $(5,1)$). Gravity only depresses the trajectory below this line, so no finite $v$ can reach $Q$ (only $v\to\infty$). Any claimed finite $v$ is FALSE.

pitfalls: In (C), assuming a flatter angle delays the peak past Q without computing $x_{max}$.
In (D), not noticing the projection line already passes through Q, making finite-$v$ passage impossible.
solution.final_check: (A) and (B) verified numerically; (C) gives $x_{max} \approx 3.8 < 5$; (D) impossible for finite $v$. Answer [A, B].

stem: A quasi-static cycle of a monoatomic ideal gas contains an isothermal process ($AB$), followed by an isochoric process ($BC$) and an adiabatic process ($CA$) as shown in the figure. The volumes of the gas are $V_1$ and $V_2$ at $A$ and $B$, respectively. If the cycle has heat input $Q_{in}$ and output $Q_{out}$, then the efficiency of the cycle is defined as $\eta = \dfrac{Q_{in} - Q_{out}}{Q_{in}}$. The correct statement(s) is/are: [Given: $\ln 2 \approx 0.7$]

options.A: If $V_2/V_1 = 8$, the heat released in the process $BC$ is smaller than the heat absorbed in the process $AB$.
options.B: For a given value of $V_2/V_1$, $\eta$ does not depend on the temperature of the isothermal process.
options.C: If $V_2/V_1 = 8$, then the temperature of the gas at $A$ is $4$ times the temperature of the gas at $C$.
options.D: If $V_2/V_1 = 8$, then the pressure of the gas at $A$ is $4$ times the pressure of the gas at $B$.

steps.text: Take the heat-engine orientation: $AB$ isothermal expansion $V_1\to V_2$ at $T_1$ ($Q_{in} = Q_{AB} = nRT_1\ln(V_2/V_1) > 0$), $BC$ isochoric cooling at $V_2$ ($Q_{out} = nC_v(T_1 - T_C) > 0$), $CA$ adiabatic compression back to $A$ (no heat). On the adiabat $T_C V_2^{\gamma-1} = T_1 V_1^{\gamma-1}$ with $\gamma - 1 = 2/3$.
(B) $\eta = 1 - Q_{out}/Q_{in} = 1 - \frac{(3/2)(1-(V_1/V_2)^{2/3})}{\ln(V_2/V_1)}$: the temperature $T_1$ cancels. TRUE.
(C) $T_A = T_1 = 4T_C$ from step 2. TRUE. (D) $p_A = nRT_1/V_1$, $p_B = nRT_1/V_2$, so $p_A/p_B = V_2/V_1 = 8 \ne 4$. FALSE.

pitfalls: Using $\gamma = 7/5$ (diatomic) instead of $5/3$ for the monoatomic gas.
Sign errors: $Q_{BC}$ is heat released (positive $Q_{out}$), not negative heat input.
solution.final_check: $\eta = 1 - \frac{1.5\times 0.75}{\ln 8} \approx 1 - 0.54 = 0.46$; (A),(B),(C) all check out, (D) contradicts $p_A/p_B = V_2/V_1 = 8$. Answer [A, B, C].

stem: The electric field associated with an electromagnetic wave travelling in vacuum is given by $E_0\sin(3x + 4y + \omega t)\,\hat{k}$, where $\omega$ is the angular frequency. All quantities are in SI units. The correct statement(s) about this wave is/are: [Given: speed of light in vacuum $c = 3\times10^8\ \mathrm{ms^{-1}}$.]

options.A: The wave is travelling in $-\dfrac{1}{5}(3\hat{i} + 4\hat{j})$ direction.
options.B: The magnitude of the wave vector is $0.5\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$.
options.D: The magnetic field associated with this wave is given by $\dfrac{E_0}{c}\sin(3x + 4y + \omega t)(4\hat{i} - 3\hat{j})$.

steps.text: Phase $\phi = 3x + 4y + \omega t = $ const moves with $3\,dx + 4\,dy = -\omega\,dt < 0$: the wave travels along $-\mathbf{k} = -(3\hat{i}+4\hat{j})$, i.e. in the $-(3\hat{i}+4\hat{j})/5$ direction. (A) TRUE.
(B) $|\mathbf{k}| = \sqrt{3^2+4^2} = 5\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}$, not $0.5$. FALSE.
(C) $\omega = c|\mathbf{k}| = (3\times10^8)(5) = 1.5\times10^9\ \mathrm{rad/s}$. TRUE.

(D) With $\hat{n} = -(3\hat{i}+4\hat{j})/5$: $\mathbf{B} = (\hat{n}\times\mathbf{E})/c = \frac{E_0}{5c}(-4\hat{i}+3\hat{j})\sin(3x+4y+\omega t)$. The option claims $(E_0/c)(4\hat{i}-3\hat{j})\sin(\cdots)$: wrong sign and missing the factor $1/5$. FALSE.

pitfalls: Reading the propagation direction from $+\mathbf{k}$ instead of $-\mathbf{k}$ (the phase has $+\omega t$, not $-\omega t$).
Forgetting to normalise $\hat{n}$ when computing $\mathbf{B}$ (the $1/5$ factor).
solution.final_check: $\mathbf{B}$ must satisfy $|\mathbf{B}| = |\mathbf{E}|/c$; the option's $|\mathbf{B}| = \sqrt{4^2+3^2}E_0/c = 5E_0/c \ne E_0/c$. Answer [A, C].

stem: A tank contains two immiscible liquids of densities $6\rho$ and $2\rho$. The higher density liquid is filled up to a height $L/2$ from the bottom. A thin rod of density $\rho$ and length $L$ is fully immersed and hinged at the bottom so that it can oscillate freely, as shown in the figure. If the rod is slightly disturbed from its equilibrium, the time period of small oscillations is $2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{L}{ng}}$, where $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity. The value of $n$ is:

formulas: $\tau = -\left(\int b(y)\,y\,dy - Mg\tfrac{L}{2}\right)\theta$, $b(y)$ = buoyant force per unit length

steps.text: Vertical equilibrium is stable (mean liquid density $4\rho > \rho$). Tilt the rod by small $\theta$; a vertical force $F$ at height $y$ gives torque $F\,y\sin\theta \simeq F\,y\,\theta$ about the hinge (upward forces restore, weight topples).

Buoyant force per unit length: $6\rho a g$ for $0<y<L/2$, $2\rho a g$ for $L/2<y<L$ ($a$ = cross-section). Restoring torque coefficient: $\kappa = \int_0^{L/2}6\rho ag\,y\,dy + \int_{L/2}^{L}2\rho ag\,y\,dy - (\rho aLg)(L/2)$.
Evaluating: $6\rho ag(L^2/8) + 2\rho ag(3L^2/8) - \rho agL^2/2 = \rho agL^2(3/4 + 3/4 - 1/2) = \rho aL^2 g$. With $I = \frac13(\rho aL)L^2$: $\omega^2 = \kappa/I = 3g/L$.
Hence $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/(3g)} = 2\pi\sqrt{L/(ng)}$ gives $n = 3$.

pitfalls: Omitting the weight's toppling torque (it reduces the restoring coefficient).
Using $I$ about the centre instead of about the hinge ($ML^2/3$).
solution.final_check: $\kappa = \rho aL^2g > 0$ (stable), $\omega = \sqrt{3g/L}$, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/(3g)}$. NOTE: the answer form was OCR-scrambled; $n = 3$ corresponds to $T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/(ng)}$ (if the form were $T = 2\pi n\sqrt{L/g}$, the value would be $1/\sqrt{3}$).

stem: As shown in the figure, five Carnot engines, each with efficiency $\eta$ and same number of cycles per unit time, are operating between six heat reservoirs. The amount of heat released per cycle by one engine is completely absorbed by the next engine. Consider $Q_0$ to be the amount of heat absorbed per cycle by the first engine and $W$ as the amount of total work done by all the engines per cycle, then the net efficiency of the system is found to be $\eta_{net} = \dfrac{W}{Q_0} = \dfrac{211}{243}$. The value of $\eta$ is:

steps.text: Engine $i$ absorbs $Q_{i-1}$, delivers $W_i = \eta Q_{i-1}$, and rejects $Q_i = (1-\eta)Q_{i-1}$, which the next engine fully absorbs.
Total work per cycle: $W = \sum_{i=1}^{5} \eta(1-\eta)^{i-1} Q_0 = \eta Q_0\,\frac{1-(1-\eta)^5}{1-(1-\eta)} = Q_0\,[1-(1-\eta)^5]$.
Hence $1 - \eta = 2/3$ and $\eta = 1/3 \approx 0.33$.

pitfalls: Summing only the works without tracking that each engine's input is the previous engine's rejected heat.
Misreading $\eta_{net}$ as $5\eta$ (valid only for small $\eta$).

stem: As shown in the figure, an insulated container is fitted with a thermally conducting but immovable partition ($P_1$) and a freely movable but thermally insulated piston ($P_2$). The partition $P_1$ with thermal conductivity $\kappa$, cross sectional area $A$ and width $w$ divides the container into two sections, $S_1$ and $S_2$, each containing one mole of a monoatomic gas. The piston $P_2$ moves freely such that the gas in $S_2$ is always at the atmospheric pressure. Initially, the difference between the temperatures of $S_1$ and $S_2$ is $\Delta T_0$. The time it takes for the temperature difference to become $\dfrac{\Delta T_0}{2}$ is $\dfrac{n\,w\,R}{\kappa\,A}$, where $R$ is the universal gas constant. The value of $n$ is: [Given: $\ln 2 \approx 0.7$]

steps.text: Heat current from $S_1$ to $S_2$ through $P_1$: $\dot{Q} = \kappa A(T_1-T_2)/w = \kappa A\,\Delta T/w$.

$S_1$ has fixed volume: $C_v\dot{T}_1 = -\dot{Q}$. $S_2$ is at constant (atmospheric) pressure: $C_v\dot{T}_2 = \dot{Q} - P\dot{V}_2$ with $P\dot{V}_2 = R\dot{T}_2$ (1 mole), so $(C_v + R)\dot{T}_2 = C_p\dot{T}_2 = +\dot{Q}$.

Subtracting: $\dot{(\Delta T)} = -\frac{\kappa A}{w}(\frac{1}{C_v}+\frac{1}{C_p})\Delta T$. For monoatomic gas $C_v = 3R/2$, $C_p = 5R/2$: $\frac{1}{C_v}+\frac{1}{C_p} = \frac{2}{3R}+\frac{2}{5R} = \frac{16}{15R}$.

Time constant $\tau = \frac{w}{\kappa A}\frac{15R}{16}$; halving time $t = \tau\ln 2 = \frac{15}{16}(0.7)\frac{wR}{\kappa A} = 0.65625\frac{wR}{\kappa A}$. With $t = n\,wR/(\kappa A)$: $n = 0.65625 \approx 0.66$.

pitfalls: Treating $S_2$ with $C_v$ instead of $C_p$: the moving piston does work, so heat entering $S_2$ splits between internal energy and work.
Sign error in $\dot{T}_2$ (it warms while $S_1$ cools).
solution.final_check: $n = (15/16)\ln 2 = 0.9375\times 0.7 = 0.65625 \approx 0.66$. NOTE: assumes the stated form $t = n\,wR/(\kappa A)$.

stem: A hollow, right circular cone of base radius $R$ and height $h$, with its tip at the origin is rotating about the $Z$-axis with an angular velocity $\omega$, as shown in the figure. The cone carries a total charge $Q$ uniformly distributed on its curved surface. The magnitude of magnetic field at a point $(0, 0, z)$, where $z \gg R$ and $z \gg h$, is $\dfrac{n\,\mu_0\,Q\,R^2\,\omega}{4\pi\,z^3}$. The value of $n$ is:

concepts: Magnetic dipole moment of rotating charge
Far-field of a magnetic dipole on axis

steps.text: Surface charge density $\sigma = Q/(\pi Rl)$ with slant height $l = \sqrt{R^2+h^2}$. A ring at height $z'$ has radius $r = Rz'/h$ and slant width $dl = (l/h)dz'$; charge $dq = \sigma\,2\pi r\,dl$.
Rotating at $\omega$, the ring carries current $dI = dq\,\omega/2\pi$, giving $dm = dI\,(\pi r^2) = (\omega/2)r^2\,dq = \pi\sigma\omega\,r^3\,dl$.

Integrate: $m = \pi\sigma\omega\frac{l}{h}\frac{R^3}{h^3}\int_0^h z'^3 dz' = \pi\sigma\omega R^3 l/4 = \frac{Q\omega R^2}{4}$ (using $\sigma = Q/\pi Rl$). Note $h$ cancels: the moment depends only on $Q$, $\omega$, $R$.
Far on-axis field: $B = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{2m}{z^3} = \frac{\mu_0 Q\omega R^2}{8\pi z^3} = \frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\mu_0 Q R^2\omega}{4\pi z^3}$. Hence $n = 1/2 = 0.50$.

pitfalls: Using the base radius $R$ for every ring instead of the local radius $r = Rz'/h$.
Forgetting the dipole far-field factor $2m$ (vs $m$) on the axis.
solution.final_check: $m = Q\omega R^2/4$; $B = (\mu_0/4\pi)(2m/z^3) = \mu_0Q\omega R^2/(8\pi z^3)$. NOTE: assumes the stated normalisation $n\mu_0QR^2\omega/(4\pi z^3)$, giving $n = 0.50$.
